# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-26 (Extended v180)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to summer Year 7. Primary locations include Paris—Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Chargemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue du Pont-aux-Choux, Rue de Thorigny, Marché Saint-Jean, Rue des Billettes, Rue Saint-Denis, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Rue de la Petite-Truanderie, Rue Mondétour, Pointe Saint-Eustache, Rue du Cygne, Rue des Prêcheurs, Rue Blomet, Rue de Rivoli, Place Louis XV, Champs-Élysées, Esplanade, bridge of the Invalides, Hôtel des Princes, Hôtel Meurice, Rue Saint-Honoré, Passage Delorme, Place du Palais-Royal, Rue de Béthisy, Rue des Bourdonnais, Rue de la Poterie, Rue du Contrat-Social, Marché-aux-Poirées, Rue de Babylone, Rue du Chaume, Rue des Vieilles-Haudriettes, Royal Printing Establishment. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Dunstead, Wilholt, Torton, Quenford, Pontoise, Stenenridge, Gulhaven.

**Rumored claims (unverified)**: Yera Stenworth confided fire at Dunstead granary set deliberately (winter Year 5). Fenelle Lindmere and Marald confided/revealed Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family. Stenenridge mill ledger rewritten after flood (autumn Year 6).

**Established facts**: Kassa Brackick and Volan Stenworth married at Staveford; Kassa later went to Dungate. Taric Corrley quit Staveford, took lodgings in Dungate. Marald Corrford quit Dunstead, took lodgings in Salcombe; Fenelle Lindmere followed within month. Ismira Stenson quit Dungate, took lodgings in Elmhaven (winter Year 6). Matho Stenson went to Elmhaven (winter Year 6). Elra Corrford settled in Elmhaven. Havie Prydenridge promised Gadrek Prydenridge to pay old debt to Stenworth family. Thizek Stenenridge told Elra Corrford deed to Kelmere pastures was forged. Kassa Stenson's husband gave solemn promise to rebuild fallen wall at Ostcombe.

**Solemn promises (established)**: Elra Corrford gave Matho Stenson solemn promise to plant orchard on slope above Gulhaven. Pelia gave Fenelle solemn promise to plant orchard on slope above Salcombe (summer Year 7).

**New births and marriages (Spring Year 7)**: Rinelle Corrley and Kadrek Brackick had son Movus Brackick (Wilholt). Nerine Prydenridge and Lurald Stenworth wed at Ostcombe with half parish present, lived in Ostcombe thereafter, had son Istho Stenworth (Ostcombe). Wenelle Lindmere and Rovus Prydenridge had son Febin Prydenridge (Kelmere). Bremira Corrford and Zavus Prydenridge married at Dunstead (before summer Year 7), lived in Dunstead thereafter.

**Spring Year 7 observations**: Multiple residents walked long way to avoid muddy square. Road rutted and puddled after thaw. Someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall. Residents hummed childhood tunes while scrubbing steps (Yera, Rinelle, Zavus, Kadan, Bremira). Matho, Bremira, and Thizek each counted coins twice, came up penny short. Taric remarked river was up at Dungate crossing; Kassa said it always was in spring. Ismira and Bremira each argued with carter over price of sack of oats. Kadan and Rovus talked of weather, harvest, lame horse. Rovus and Kadan discussed scandal of salt prices. Bremira and Ferald discussed scandal of salt prices. Yera laughed at story nobody else found funny. Yera Stenworth and Zavus complained of aching backs. Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage. Gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps. Children chased hoop down lane. Lurald and Ilrald discussed weather, harvest, lame horse. Isvie and Ferald Stenworth talked of weather, harvest, lame horse.

**Summer Year 7 observations**: Frost silvered hedges overnight. Rain threatened since morning but held off. Smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields. Someone chalked crooked sun on wall of forge (repeated observation). Sebin remarked river was up; Rorald Lindmere said it always was in spring. Pelia watched clouds, predicted rain wrongly. Rorald fell asleep in chair before fire caught. Sebin and Rorald Lindmere both laughed at stories nobody else found funny. Children chased hoop down lane. Light went early. Pelia complained of aching back, as usual. Dog barked at nothing then went quiet. Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. Pelia counted coins twice, came up penny short. Yewyn Haskick bought ribbon at stall and regretted it. Tatho Brackick bought ribbon at stall and regretted it. Pelia remarked price of salt scandal; Tatho agreed. Yewyn appeared tired; Pelia noted this.

**Summer Year 7 broken faith**: Rorald Lindmere broke faith with Kassa Stenson—promised work (carry sealed letter to Torton) never begun.

## Jean Valjean's Crisis and Discovery
**Blotting-book discovery (night 24th June 1832)**: Upon arriving at Rue de l'Homme Armé lodgings, Valjean found Cosette's blotting-book open on sideboard. Mirror reflection revealed four lines—letter Cosette wrote to young workman in Rue Plumet. **Valjean's collapse**: Understood Cosette was escaping; another was goal of her heart. Soul gave utter roar. **Nature of his paternal love**: Into paternity his life's widowhood introduced all shades of love—daughter, mother, sister, woman, wife. **Spiritual crisis**: Grief surpassed bounds; quiver of revolt ran head to foot; immense reawakening of egotism; the *I* howled.

**During Spring Year 7**: Groped up stairs, hand trembling greatly. Unfolded Marius's note announcing death and love. Seized essential points. Beheld splendor of death of hated individual, remained crushed with intoxicated amazement. **Rue de l'Homme Armé lodgings**: Two sleeping-rooms, dining-room, kitchen, garret for Toussaint on second floor, back court. Initially slept well; awoke almost gay; recovered serenity and security. Twice or thrice Toussaint stammered about fighting in Paris—Valjean paid no heed, absorbed in calculations.

**Current state (summer Year 7)**: Valjean asleep; Toussaint has not risen. Cosette's father thought unkind by her.

## Marius and Cosette's Romance
**Recognition and love**: Cosette acknowledged she never forgot Marius, always loved him. Beginning autumn Year 5, Marius came every evening, forcing old gate. At height of love's voluptuousness, remained absolutely chaste. **Confessions (spring Year 6, during cholera)**: Marius told Cosette—orphan, name Marius Pontmercy, lawyer, father colonel and hero on bad terms with rich grandfather, hinted at being baron. Cosette told Marius—brought up at Petit-Picpus convent, mother dead, father M. Fauchelevent. **Éponine's death (evening 24th June)**: Éponine revealed she led Marius to barricade, spoke of her death as blessing, protected him from gunfire. Gave Marius letter from Cosette before dying. **Cosette's letter content**: Marriage impossible; grandfather refuses; no fortune either; hastened to him, he gone; kept promise given; dies; loves him. **Marius's response**: Covered letter with kisses; reflected Cosette going to England. Resolved to inform Cosette of death, send farewell, save Gavroche.

**Marius joins barricade (evening 24th June)**: Upon learning Valjean plans England departure in one week, arranged meeting 26th June at nine o'clock. Same evening, displaced bar at grating, rushed in. Cosette absent. Seated self with resolution, blessed love. Mad with grief, one desire: speedy end. Voice summoned him to barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie. **Philosophy of duty**: Reflected on Colonel Pontmercy—proud soldier, guarded frontier. Own day come; must follow father, show bravery, seek death. Carries loaded pistols. **During first phase**: Witnessed M. Mabeuf's death, Bahorel killed; flung self into conflict. Saved Gavroche with first shot, delivered Courfeyrac with second. Seized powder barrel, dropped flame with startling cry. **Mental state (6th June, dawn)**: Fasting, fevered, emerged from all hope, stranded in grief, saturated with violent emotions, conscious end was near, plunged into visionary stupor voluntarily accepted. Despair's ecstasy. Felt he had entered tomb.

**Cosette's current state (summer Year 7, morning)**: Slept only few hours but soundly; had sweet dreams. Awoke with sun in eyes. First thought smiling. Felt thoroughly reassured. Like Valjean, passed through reaction of soul that absolutely will not hear of unhappiness. Began cherishing hope without knowing why. Then felt pang at heart. Three days since saw Marius. Said to herself: he must have received her letter, knows where she is, clever enough to find means of reaching her. Certain he would come today, perhaps this very morning. Felt she could not live without Marius. Youth quickly dries eyes, finds sorrow useless, does not accept it. Youth is smile of future in presence of unknown quantity. Natural to it to be happy. Respiration made of hope. Could not remember what Marius said about one-day absence or explanation he gave. Vexed at memory's failure; told herself naughty and wicked to forget Marius's words. Dressed hastily, combed hair. Opened window, looked around hoping to see street, angle of house, edge of pavement to watch for Marius. No view of outside; back court surrounded by high walls, outlook only on gardens. Pronounced gardens hideous; for first time found flowers ugly. Smallest scrap of street gutter would meet wishes better. Decided to gaze at sky, thought Marius might come from that quarter. Then burst into tears. Not fickleness; hopes cut in twain by dejection. Confused consciousness of something horrible. Thoughts rife in air. Told herself not sure of anything, withdrawal from sight meant being lost. Idea Marius could return from heaven no longer charming but mournful. Counted on Marius. Eclipse of such light decidedly impossible. Heard sharp shocks in distance, thought people opening and shutting carriage gates early—actually cannon reports battering barricade.

## Barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie (24th June into 6th June)
**Café Corinthe**: Ground floor with bar; first floor with billiard-table and spiral staircase; cellar via trap-door; lodgings and attics. Proprietor: Widow Hucheloup. Serving-maids: Matelote, Gibelotte. **Two barricades**: Larger shut off Rue de la Chanvrerie; other closed Rue Mondétour. **Larger barricade (6th June, dawn)**: Height six or seven feet, stepped construction, paling-stones, casks, wheels, omnibus pole with ropes, red flag. Forty-three insurgents. **Three-front fortification**: Walled on Rue de la Chanvrerie (front), Rues du Cygne and de la Petite Truanderie (left), Rue Mondétour (right). Almost impregnable but fatally hemmed in. No exit.

**Javert's arrest**: Identified as Inspector of Police, aged fifty-two. Bound with whip-cord about feet, martingale rope from neck. Upon seeing Valjean surveying him, remarked: "It is perfectly simple."

**Le Cabuc execution**: Enjolras executed him for killing, justified by insurrection needing discipline.

**M. Mabeuf's sacrifice**: Venerable, austere, aged eighty. Evening 24th June: followed band, refused arms. During attack: tore flag from Enjolras, upholding red banner with aged arm. Enjolras eulogized: magnificent death; presence renders barricade impregnable. Body lay in kitchen on table.

**Unknown messenger (6th June, dawn)**: Some unknown blouse-wearer appeared, announced with inexorable resolution: whole army of Paris striking, third of army bearing down, National Guard advancing, attack in one hour. Never known name of this man.

**After first assault and repairs**: Insurgents rallied, majority ascended to first-story window. Medical students cared for wounded. Five gravely wounded men on mattresses in kitchen converted to ambulance. Barricade repaired and augmented, raised two feet.

**Provisions and morale (6th June, dawn)**: No repast possible. Fifty men exhausted scanty provisions during sixteen hours. Fifteen full bottles hermetically sealed found in cellar. Enjolras placed veto on them. Insurgents full of hope, smiled waiting for dawn attack, reckoned succor on way, divided day into three phases: six o'clock—regiment would turn; noon—insurrection of all Paris; sunset—revolution.

**First cannon attack (6th June)**: A stir began in Saint-Leu quarter. Clashing of chains, uneasy jolting, click of brass announced sinister construction of iron approaching. Cannoneers rolled cannon into position facing barricade without haste, gravity of astronomer. Captain began to point cannon. Whole barricade fired, report terrible; avalanche of smoke covered both cannon and men. After few seconds cloud dispersed; not one cannon crew member struck. Flame leaped forth from insurgent rifle. Artillery-man turned round twice, arms extended, head uplifted as though for breath, then fell with side on gun, motionless. Back showed stream of blood. Ball traversed breast from side to side. Dead. After sergeant's death, exasperated troop lying flat on stomachs behind line of paving-stones opened fire on barricade. Insurgents did not reply to spare ammunition.

**Mattress incident**: Old woman, foreseeing bullets, placed mattress in front of attic window on roof of six-story house slightly beyond barricade. Mattress placed cross-wise, supported at bottom on two poles for drying linen, upheld at top by two ropes attached to nails in window frames. Ropes distinctly visible like hairs against sky. Mattress fell outside barricade between besiegers and besieged.

**Cannon specifications**: Piece of eight, new model, brass. Subject to bursting if tin proportion exceeded. May need hooping with unwedded steel bands to strengthen. Gribeauval's movable star offers better method. Augments projectile force but diminishes accuracy. Rifled cannon of sixteenth century had defects from small charges. At short range trajectory not rigid as desired; parabola exaggerated. Cannon-ball travels six hundred leagues per hour; light travels seventy thousand leagues per second—superiority of Jesus Christ over Napoleon.

**Gavroche's lie about Cosette's letter (6th June, dawn)**: In haste to return to barricade, Gavroche got rid of letter rather than delivered it. Confided lightly to stranger whose face he could not make out. Man was bareheaded but insufficient. Administered little inward remonstrances; feared Marius's reproaches. To extricate from predicament, lied abominably.

## Philosophical Discussions (6th June, barricade)
Combeferre quoted and discussed classical figures—Harmodius and Aristogiton, Brutus, Chereas, Stephanus, Cromwell, Charlotte Corday, Sand. Compared translators of Georgics. Discussion reverted to Brutus and Cæsar. Combeferre argued Cæsar fell justly; Cæsar violated Rubicon, conferred dignities as though from himself, not rising at senate entrance. His twenty-three wounds touch less than spitting in face of Jesus Christ. Cæsar stabbed by senators; Christ cuffed by lackeys. One feels God through greater outrage. **Combeferre on war and kings**: When no more kings, there will be no more war. Hideous butcheries. Remarked sergeant was charming young man, intrepid, thoughtful, well-educated, probably in love, not more than five and twenty, might be someone's brother.
